messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is a 55-year-old African American man who has worked for years as a house painter, moving from room to room with a radio on low and the smell of primer and thinner in the air. He came to treatment after the sudden death of a loved one, a loss that had split his life into a clear before and after. The death had unfolded in an emergency setting, and what remains most searing is not a calm narrative but flashes: the ambulance lights, the sound of urgent voices, the sense that everything was happening too fast while he could do nothing to stop it. Even now, when he tries to speak about that day, he does not always get a full scene. Sometimes the feeling arrives first and all at once—raw grief and panic with no clear picture attached—and at other times what comes are stark visual fragments, like still photographs he cannot control.

In the weeks after the death, ordinary parts of life began to take on the charge of that day. Seeing an ambulance on the street could make his whole body tighten before he had even fully registered what he was looking at. At work, being on a job site became difficult in ways that embarrassed him. If a coworker mentioned someone who had lost a spouse, parent, or child, Kwame would go quiet and feel himself leave the conversation internally, as if he were already back in the emotional weather of the loss. The workplace itself became a setting he dreaded; climbing ladders and painting trim in clients’ homes, he found himself listening for sirens outside and scanning for signs that something terrible was about to happen. Those moments did more than upset him. They left him feeling that his life had been shattered beyond repair, and that other people were still moving through an intact world from which he had been cut off.

As these reactions persisted, Kwame had come to believe that he was no longer the man he had been before. He described feeling as if he did not know himself anymore: a man who used to work steadily, talk easily, and return home tired but settled now moved through his days braced and estranged. That sense of being altered fed his watchfulness. He was certain something in him had changed permanently, and because of that he no longer trusted his surroundings, even in his own house. Nights were the worst. Daylight offered distraction, but after dark he felt exposed, tense, and unable to let down his guard. He checked doors, listened for sounds outside, and stayed keyed up long after his wife had gone to bed.

His view of himself and his life also shaped the way the loss stayed in his mind. Because he saw the event as having destroyed his life, any return of memory seemed to confirm it. When images surfaced, they were not just recollections; they felt like proof that he was trapped in the worst moment of his life. And when no image came, only the same crushing emotional force, that too reinforced his sense that the loss had taken over from the inside, beyond his control. The more isolated he felt from others, the less likely he was to talk, and the less he talked, the more the memories remained unprocessed, returning as pictures, surges of grief, or sudden emotional collapses without warning.

A tightening pattern gradually took hold. When Kwame felt on guard at home or caught himself tensing at night, the heightened alertness itself seemed to pull the trauma closer. In that state, his mind became quick to latch onto ambulance sirens in the distance, conversations about bereavement, or reminders at work that might otherwise have passed him by. Once activated, those cues brought back the images and the unbearable grief, and the memories in turn made his body feel even more ready for danger. After a bad night he would go to work already braced, and because he was scanning so hard for threat, the workplace felt full of reminders. By the end of the day he would think, again, that this was all his life was now: a man set apart, a man ruined by what happened.

Over time he withdrew socially, not because he had lost interest in people in a general way, but because talk of illness, death, or family emergencies had become so potent that he could not stay present for it. His wife noticed he was harder to reach and more restless after dark. He began to fear not only the memories themselves but the places and moments that might call them up, and the more that happened, the more convinced he became that nowhere was truly safe. He finally sought help when he realized he was dreading both home at night and the job sites where he had spent most of his adult life. What frightens him most is the thought that the loss has permanently destroyed who he is. What he hopes, cautiously, is that he might learn how to be in his own home, hear an ambulance, or stand at work without feeling pulled back into that day.
